# **The AllSet Multiset Learning Framework: Theoretical Foundations, Algorithmic Complexity, and Adaptability for Temporal Provenance Graphs**

## **Introduction to Higher-Order Graph Representation Learning**

Graph-centered machine learning, particularly through the deployment of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs), has fundamentally altered the landscape of relational data modeling. The ubiquity of graph-structured data has led to the widespread adoption of these models across disciplines ranging from quantum chemistry and structural biology to social network analysis and recommendation systems.1 However, standard graph formulations are mathematically restricted to modeling strictly pairwise interactions between entities. This dyadic restriction severely limits their utility and representational capacity in complex, real-world systems where interactions naturally involve three or more agents simultaneously.1 Hypergraphs, a profound structural generalization of standard graphs, overcome this foundational limitation by allowing edges—termed hyperedges—to encapsulate an arbitrary number of nodes simultaneously. This higher-order mathematical formulation is highly adept at capturing group-wise relationships, such as multi-protein complexes in biological networks, joint authorship in academic citations, or multi-entity interactions within software execution provenance logs.3  
Despite the profound theoretical advantages of hypergraphs over simple graphs, developing computationally efficient, mathematically stable, and highly expressive neural architectures for hypergraph-structured data has proven historically challenging.3 Until recently, the machine learning community predominantly approached this problem by forcefully converting hypergraphs back into standard graphs through heuristic propagation rules—such as clique expansion and star expansion—or by utilizing mathematically complex but computationally rigid tensor-based methodologies.1 These legacy methods consistently demonstrated suboptimal performance on rigorous benchmarking datasets because they inherently lose the nuance of higher-order interactions, introduce massive computational overhead, or suffer from severe oversmoothing during deep layer propagation.1  
To resolve the structural limitations of heuristic-based hypergraph convolutions, the "AllSet" framework was introduced as a highly general, uniquely expressive paradigm that models hypergraph neural network layers as a composition of two distinct multiset functions.3 By radically redefining hypergraph message passing as bipartite multiset learning, AllSet fundamentally altered the field. It represents the first architecture to successfully integrate deep learning advances in set function approximation—specifically Deep Sets and Set Transformers—with hypergraph neural networks.1 The ensuing analysis provides an exhaustive, mathematically rigorous deconstruction of the AllSet framework, detailing its message passing formulation, attention mechanisms, computational complexity, and theoretical subsumption of prior methodologies. Furthermore, this report extracts the core tenets of the AllSet architecture to design a comprehensive blueprint for adapting bipartite multiset message passing to the domain of temporal provenance graphs, specifically addressing the replacement of static structural attention with temporal state-space transitions.

## **Mathematical Formulations of Hypergraphs and the Limitations of Prior Paradigms**

To rigorously understand the architectural superiority of the AllSet paradigm, it is imperative to first establish the formal mathematical definitions of hypergraph structures and analyze the critical failings of the methodologies that preceded it. The foundational nomenclature and linear algebra underpinning hypergraph theory serve as the baseline against which all modern advancements are measured.  
A hypergraph is formally defined as an ordered pair ![][image1], where ![][image2] denotes the universal set of nodes (or vertices), and ![][image3] represents the set of hyperedges. Unlike a standard graph edge, which is strictly restricted to a 2-element subset of ![][image4], a hyperedge ![][image5] is an arbitrary subset of ![][image4], such that ![][image6].1 If every hyperedge in the network contains exactly ![][image7] nodes, the hypergraph is termed ![][image7]\-uniform, which can be elegantly represented by a ![][image7]\-dimensional supersymmetric tensor.1 However, empirical real-world data is almost never perfectly uniform. Interactions inherently vary in scale, from bipartite connections to massive systemic events encompassing hundreds of entities.  
Consequently, the most robust structural representation of an arbitrary, non-uniform hypergraph is its incidence matrix, denoted as ![][image8].9 The incidence matrix explicitly maps the exact, uncorrupted relationships between the node set and the hyperedge set. An element ![][image9] if node ![][image10] is a constituent of hyperedge ![][image11] (i.e., ![][image12]), and ![][image13] otherwise.2 From this incidence matrix, one can derive two critical diagonal matrices: the node degree matrix ![][image14] where the ![][image15]\-th diagonal element is the sum of the ![][image15]\-th row of ![][image16], and the hyperedge degree matrix ![][image17] where the ![][image18]\-th diagonal element is the sum of the ![][image18]\-th column of ![][image16].9

### **The Fallacy of Graph Reductions: Clique, Star, and Line Expansions**

Prior to the formalization of the AllSet paradigm, the standard methodology for executing spatial or spectral convolutions on hypergraphs relied heavily on structural reduction techniques, primarily Clique Expansion (CE), Star Expansion (SE), and Line Expansion.  
Clique Expansion forcefully reduces a hypergraph into a weighted standard graph by projecting the incidence matrix onto itself. Mathematically, the adjacency matrix of the clique-expanded graph is approximated as ![][image19], where ![][image20] is a diagonal matrix of hyperedge weights.1 This heuristic methodology suffers from severe structural information loss. By forcing a hyperedge into a clique, the model erroneously treats a singular, holistic group interaction as a collection of independent, pairwise interactions.1 This introduces massive information redundancy and false positive structural relationships, diluting the semantic meaning of the original multi-entity event.12  
Star expansion mitigates some clique-expansion noise by introducing a new bipartite structure where hyperedges become virtual nodes, but traditional implementations often failed to parameterize the distinct semantic differences between the original nodes and the virtual hyperedge nodes appropriately, leading to oversmoothing. Line expansion preserves homogeneity because all nodes in the resulting graph represent "node-hyperedge" pairs, but this expansion leads to a substantially large graph, significantly increasing both computational and space complexity well beyond viable limits for massive datasets.12  
Models such as HGNN and HyperGCN inherently rely on these reductive paradigms, attempting to map hypergraph learning into classical spectral graph convolution via the normalized hypergraph Laplacian.1 While spectral methods ensure mathematical stability and are grounded in solid signal processing theory, they forcefully homogenize the multi-agent nature of the data, severely bottlenecking the model's capacity to learn complex, non-linear dependencies.

### **The Intractability of Tensor-Based Propagations**

To avoid the noise introduced by clique expansion, alternative methodologies explored tensor-based propagations, attempting to solve the ![][image21]\-eigenproblem or ![][image16]\-eigenproblem directly on the multi-dimensional tensor representation of the hypergraph.1 The ![][image21]\-eigenproblem for an adjacency tensor ![][image22] of a ![][image7]\-uniform hypergraph is defined mathematically as ![][image23], where the tensor multiplication captures the true high-order structural dependency.2  
While these methods theoretically preserve higher-order interactions faithfully and demonstrate performance gains in specific clustering tasks, they scale abysmally in deep learning environments. Computing tensor eigenproblems is highly computationally complex, scaling exponentially with the uniformity degree. Furthermore, defining propagation rules based on ![][image16]\-eigenproblems can frequently lead to the generation of imaginary feature vectors, which are deeply problematic for standard neural network gradient descent optimizations and activation functions.1 Therefore, both graph-reduction heuristics and pure tensor algebra proved insufficient for generalized, scalable hypergraph representation learning.

## **The AllSet Paradigm: Bipartite Message Passing and Multiset Functions**

The theoretical breakthrough of the AllSet framework lies in decisively abandoning both the destructive graph-reduction heuristics of clique expansion and the computational intractability of tensor eigenproblems. Instead, AllSet reframes the hypergraph explicitly as a bipartite graph consisting of two distinct, non-overlapping node sets: the original entities ![][image4] and the hyperedges ![][image24] treated as independent, feature-rich "virtual nodes".6 In this bipartite perspective, directed messages flow exclusively between nodes and the hyperedges they belong to, maintaining the exact, uncorrupted topology of the original incidence matrix ![][image16] without generating false pairwise cliques.  
Because a hyperedge is structurally defined as a collection of nodes, and a node's local neighborhood is structurally defined as a collection of hyperedges, the aggregation of information in this bipartite structure must operate on collections of elements. In highly connected networks, elements in these collections may repeat depending on the specific propagation depth or multiplexed connections. Therefore, the AllSet authors mathematically formalized hypergraph convolution as the composition of two multiset functions.1

### **Permutation Invariance and the Bipartite Propagation Rule**

A multiset is a generalization of a standard mathematical set that allows for multiple instances of the multiset's elements. A multiset function is a specialized mapping that takes a multiset as input and produces a vector representation, subject to the strict architectural requirement of permutation invariance.1 Permutation invariance mandates that the output of the function remains mathematically identical regardless of the order in which the elements of the multiset are processed or stored in memory. This is critical for hypergraphs, as the nodes within a hyperedge (e.g., the participants in a meeting) have no inherent sequential ordering.  
The core message passing formulation of AllSet defines two distinct, learnable multiset functions. Let ![][image25] represent the node feature matrix at propagation step ![][image26], and ![][image27] represent the intermediate hyperedge feature matrix. The AllSet message passing formulation is expressed through the following bipartite equations:

1. **Node-to-Hyperedge Aggregation (![][image28]):**  
   Each hyperedge ![][image29] aggregates the features of all its constituent nodes ![][image30]. This forms the latent representation of the hyperedge itself based on the current state of its participants.

2. **Hyperedge-to-Node Aggregation (![][image36]):**  
   Subsequently, each node ![][image34] aggregates the newly computed features of all hyperedges ![][image29] that it is incident to (denoted as ![][image37]). This updates the node's state based on all the higher-order interactions it participated in.

By defining the hypergraph neural network layer exclusively as the composition of ![][image40], AllSet establishes a fully generalized framework.1 The expressivity of the resulting hypergraph neural network is thus entirely bottlenecked by—and conversely, unlocked by—the expressivity of the specific multiset functions chosen to parameterize the aggregations.

## **Algorithmic Instantiations of the AllSet Framework**

To achieve maximum modeling flexibility and high expressive power, the AllSet framework must parameterize the multiset functions ![][image28] and ![][image36] using neural architectures that are proven universal approximators of set functions.1 Drawing on recent advances in deep learning regarding sequence-agnostic processing, the framework is instantiated in two primary forms: AllDeepSets and AllSetTransformer.1

While AllDeepSets is mathematically proven to be a universal approximator given sufficiently wide MLPs, empirical and theoretical analyses indicate that the unweighted summation operation inside the Deep Sets module creates a significant representational bottleneck in practice.1 Unweighted summation forces the inner ![][image46] to map input features into a highly specific latent space where simple first-order statistics (like sums) can effectively differentiate between distinct, overlapping multisets.5 In highly dense hypergraphs where multiple complex subsets interact in convoluted ways, a simple summation fails to appropriately weigh the relative importance of specific nodes within a hyperedge, leading to gradient vanishing or feature homogenization during training.

## **Deep Dive into the AllSetTransformer Attention Mechanism**

The specific attention mechanism deployed in the AllSetTransformer represents a massive leap in hypergraph feature representation, particularly regarding how information is prioritized during the bipartite message passing flow.  
In prior attention-based methodologies such as Hypergraph Convolution and Hypergraph Attention (HCHA), attention coefficients were computed using static heuristics or specific node-edge feature combinations that failed entirely if the dataset lacked explicit, pre-computed hyperedge features.2 The attention weights in HCHA relied on combining node features and pre-existing hyperedge domain features, a luxury not afforded by many sparse or organically derived datasets.  
In stark contrast, the AllSetTransformer utilizes an induced set attention mechanism that organically learns the relative importance of entities strictly from the topology and node features. When computing the message from nodes to a hyperedge (![][image28]), the multiset ![][image41] consists of the node features ![][image65] for all ![][image30]. The learnable matrix ![][image47] acts as a geometric anchor or a "prototypical" query for the target concept. The inner product ![][image66] computes the similarity between the abstract, learned optimal query space and the actual features of the nodes within the specific hyperedge.  
The application of the softmax function normalizes these similarity scores into a continuous probability distribution across the nodes. Consequently, the attention mechanism effectively learns to weight the importance of different constituent nodes dynamically. If a particular hyperedge represents a research paper, and its nodes represent cited authors, the attention mechanism isolates the most semantically dense, influential authors and down-weights secondary co-authors, entirely bypassing the requirement for pre-calculated TF-IDF weights or manual graph filtering.  
When the flow reverses for the hyperedge-to-node propagation (![][image36]), a separate Set Transformer layer utilizes a new, independently learnable query ![][image67]. Here, the multiset ![][image41] is the collection of hyperedges incident to the target node. The attention mechanism dynamically evaluates which hyperedges (events or groups) are most influential in defining the state of the target node, outputting an anisotropically weighted sum of hyperedge features. This effectively performs an adaptive, context-aware structural diffusion that cannot be achieved via standard clique-expansion approximations or isotopic ODE-based diffusion.7

## **Computational and Space Complexity Analysis**

A frequent, fatal failing of highly expressive neural network architectures is their computational intractability. Methods that rely on dense tensor multiplications or fully connected clique expansions routinely run out of VRAM on modern GPUs when applied to graphs with more than a few thousand nodes. However, despite its profound theoretical expressivity and reliance on complex Set Transformer modules, the AllSet framework maintains an extraordinarily efficient computational complexity profile, scaling linearly with the size of the graph's fundamental topological data structure.1  
The size of a hypergraph is governed by the number of nodes ![][image68], the number of hyperedges ![][image69], and the incidence structure. The dense incidence matrix ![][image16] has a spatial footprint of ![][image70], which grows exponentially as the network scales, rendering traditional transductive hypergraph computing methods unviable for large-scale datasets like the Walmart or Yelp networks.15 To achieve scalability, AllSet leverages the structural sparsity of the incidence matrix.  
In a sparse matrix representation, the computational cost is driven entirely by the number of non-zero entries in ![][image16], which corresponds precisely to the sum of the cardinalities of all hyperedges, ![][image71].5 This value represents the total number of bipartite edges connecting nodes to hyperedges in the unrolled computation graph.

## **Theoretical Subsumption and Comparison to Prior Methodologies**

To firmly establish the theoretical preeminence of the AllSet architecture, the authors of the framework provided rigorous mathematical proofs demonstrating that AllSet strictly subsumes a vast majority of preceding hypergraph neural networks.1 By demonstrating that prior heuristic algorithms are mere special, constrained cases of the generalized ![][image28] and ![][image36] framework, AllSet proves that its expressive power is a mathematical upper bound on current state-of-the-art spatial methods.  
The theoretical subsumption hierarchy can be summarized through the rigorous analysis of specific baseline models and their restrictive aggregation paradigms:

| Model | Node → Hyperedge Aggregation | Hyperedge → Node Aggregation | Relation to AllSet Framework & Limitations Overcome |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **HGNN** 2 | ![][image84] | ![][image85] | A highly constrained variant of AllDeepSets. It utilizes fixed degree normalizations (![][image86]) and single linear projections instead of unconstrained, deep MLPs. It overcomes HGNN's inability to learn non-linear intra-edge interactions. |
| **HyperGCN** 5 | ![][image87] | ![][image88] | Limits the node-to-hyperedge multiset function to a simple, non-learnable max pooling operator. This severely bottlenecked information flow, ignoring the contributions of all but the single most prominent node. AllSet utilizes all node data intelligently. |
| **HCHA** 5 | ![][image89] | ![][image90] | Employs attention but is bottlenecked by the requirement of explicit topological or external features to compute ![][image91]. HCHA is effectively a constrained, less flexible version of AllSetTransformer. |
| **HyperSAGE** 1 | ![][image92] | ![][image93] | Adapts GraphSAGE directly, restricting multiset functions to unweighted mean-aggregators. This utterly fails to capture non-uniform feature importance, treating every node and every incident hyperedge equally. AllSet dynamically weights importance. |
| **UniGNN** 5 | ![][image94] | ![][image95] | A unified framework extending GNNs, but still relies on unweighted summation and residual linear projections. Subsumed by the far more expressive MLPs within AllDeepSets. |

According to Theorem 3.4 of the framework's foundational proofs, architectures such as HGNN, HCHA, HNHN, HyperSAGE, and HyperGCN are restricted, lower-capacity formulations.1 They utilize fixed aggregators (sum, mean, max) or rigid degree-based normalizations that map to highly specific, inflexible multiset functions. By stripping away these heuristics and replacing them with universal approximators (Deep Sets and Set Transformers), AllSet naturally encompasses these legacy algorithms.1 Furthermore, AllSet is uniquely capable of capturing the sophisticated anisotropic propagation dynamics characteristic of tensor-based ![][image21]\-eigenproblem algorithms, a feat rigorously proven to be entirely impossible for CE-based neural networks.2

### **Empirical Benchmarking Performance**

The theoretical superiority of AllSet is robustly validated by extensive empirical benchmarking. The framework was evaluated across 13 diverse datasets, ranging from standard citation networks (Cora, Citeseer, Pubmed) and co-authorship graphs (Cora-CA, DBLP-CA) to highly complex object classification (ModelNet40) and massive review networks (Yelp, Walmart).2  
To provide context on the scale, the Yelp dataset contains over 50,000 nodes and 316,000 hyperedges, while the Walmart dataset exceeds 88,000 nodes and 69,000 hyperedges.2 Across these rigorous benchmarks, AllSetTransformer consistently matched or outperformed all other hypergraph neural networks. On the most challenging datasets, AllSet demonstrated unique performance leaps, achieving close to a 4% accuracy improvement over existing methods on the Yelp and Zoo datasets, and a 3% improvement on the Walmart dataset.1 The empirical evidence confirms that framing hypergraph learning as bipartite multiset learning is not merely a theoretical exercise, but the definitive state-of-the-art methodology for higher-order representation learning.

## **Adaptation Blueprint: Temporal Provenance Graphs and State-Space Transitions**

The architectural structure of the AllSet framework provides a highly optimized, mathematically sound blueprint for processing complex, multi-agent interactions. While AllSet was initially evaluated on standard, static hypergraph node-classification benchmarks, its bipartite multiset formulation is the exact mathematical skeleton required for modeling and analyzing Temporal Provenance Graphs.  
In systems security, digital forensics, and data tracking, a provenance graph details the exact causal execution history of a computer system. The fundamental topology of a provenance graph natively aligns with a hypergraph structure, diverging sharply from standard pairwise graphs:

* **Entities (Nodes, ![][image4]):** The fundamental, persistent objects within the system. Examples include executable processes, data files, network sockets, or memory pipes.  
* **Events (Hyperedges, ![][image24]):** The causal actions or system calls that occur within the system. A system event rarely involves just two entities. For instance, an event where a parent process fork()s a child process, which simultaneously reads a configuration file and opens a network socket, is a singular, atomic higher-order interaction binding four distinct entities simultaneously.

To effectively parse temporal provenance graphs for anomaly detection or threat hunting, we must adapt the AllSet framework, bridging the gap between static topological analysis and dynamic, time-series causality.

### **Mapping Provenance Entities and Events to Bipartite Multiset Frameworks**

The fundamental structure of the provenance adaptation retains the AllSet bipartite graph in its entirety, as it flawlessly models the entity-event dichotomy. The mathematical propagation operates as follows:

1. **Entity-to-Event Aggregation (![][image96]):**  
   When a system event occurs, the latent representations of all input entities (e.g., the acting process, the read file) must be aggregated to form the latent representation of the event itself. This captures the state of the participating objects *at the moment of the event*.  
2. **Event-to-Entity Aggregation (![][image97]):**  
   Once the event's latent state is computed, this causal information must flow forward into the output entities (e.g., the written file, the spawned process), updating their latent states to reflect the direct consequences and systemic ripple effects of the event.

However, a critical incompatibility exists. While the AllSetTransformer is highly effective for static graphs where the entire topology exists simultaneously, standard Set Transformer attention is symmetric and inherently time-agnostic. In a provenance graph, events are strictly causal and ordered continuously across a temporal axis, ![][image98]. Therefore, the static multiset functions of AllSet must be structurally augmented to preserve the arrow of time and causal dependency.

### **Replacing Static Attention with Temporal State-Space Transitions**

The architectural breakthrough required for temporal provenance graphs is the modification of the AllSetTransformer's attention query vector, ![][image47]. In the standard AllSet framework, ![][image47] is a universally learned, static parameter that remains fixed across the entire graph during inference.1 To adapt this for provenance tracking, the static attention query must be replaced by a temporal State-Space transition.  
Instead of a static ![][image47], the architecture will maintain a dynamic, continuously updating system state vector, ![][image99]. This state vector is governed by a continuous or discretized State-Space Model (SSM), such as those utilized in highly efficient sequential architectures like Mamba or S4. The state vector ![][image99] acts as a rolling memory of the entire system's execution context up to time ![][image26].  
When a provenance event ![][image100] occurs at timestamp ![][image26], the entity-to-event multiset function (![][image96]) utilizes the current system state ![][image99] as the query vector to evaluate the participating entities. If the rolling system state ![][image99] indicates suspicious preliminary activity (e.g., a potential malware intrusion attempting privilege escalation), the query vector ![][image104] dynamically shifts to pay maximum attention to high-risk entities (like network sockets or system binaries) within the multiset of the current event. The attention is no longer static; it is contextually reactive.

This ensures that a file written to during a malicious event carries the "taint" of that event forward in its individual feature vector.

### **Preserving Linear Complexity in Temporal Tracking**

Crucially, this temporal adaptation perfectly preserves the linear computational complexity of the original AllSet paradigm.5 Because modern state-space models (unlike standard sequence transformers) operate with strictly linear computational complexity ![][image108] with respect to the sequence length ![][image109] (the number of events), and the AllSet multiset function scales linearly with the sum of hyperedge cardinalities ![][image110], the combined architecture maintains a strict algorithmic complexity of ![][image111].  
This ensures that the mechanism remains perfectly linear. This is an absolute necessity for cyber-security and system auditing applications, allowing the architecture to seamlessly parse massive provenance logs containing millions of system calls in real-time without encountering the quadratic memory bottlenecks that plague standard temporal attention models. By replacing AllSet's static geometric queries with a rolling SSM state, the framework transitions from a spatial hypergraph classifier into a highly scalable, causally aware, temporal anomaly detection engine.
